s: A 210 m karst shaft in the Qara Mountains · home of an endangered cave fish
dr: Sinkhole (doline) in a karstified limestone plateau; not dated
el: About 210 m deep; opening about 130 × 90 m
se: A giant hole in Dhofar’s hills drops about 210 m to water where a rare pale fish lives and migrating birds come to drink
sa: حفرة عملاقة في تلال ظفار تهبط نحو 210 أمتار حتى الماء، حيث تعيش سمكة باهتة نادرة وتأتي الطيور المهاجرة لتشرب
desc: A karst sinkhole on the Qara plateau between Salalah and Mirbat, with an oval opening of about 130 × 90 m at about 680 m above sea level and a shaft about 210 m deep that narrows to about 60 m across at 100 m depth. A long wadi ends at the shaft, making it a river sink, and the groundwater table lies at its base. In 1980 British cavers collected a depigmented cyprinid fish from a pool in a side passage about 200 m down; it was described in 1987 as Garra dunsirei, known only from this sinkhole. The species is assessed as Endangered by IUCN (2015). The shaft was explored in 1997 by Slovenian cavers and members of Sultan Qaboos University.
sig: One of Arabia’s largest karst shafts and the only known home of the cave fish Garra dunsirei.
disc: Only known home of Garra dunsirei
refs: Duckeck, J. Tawi Ateer (Tawi Atair Sinkhole), Oman. Showcaves.com. https://showcaves.com/english/om/karst/TawiAteer.html
Cavefishes of the World: Garra dunsirei species record. https://cavefishes.org.uk/species-record.php?id=66
Garra dunsirei Banister, 1987. Plazi treatment. https://treatment.plazi.org/GgServer/html/03FBBC4B095BB205EC95FF4B233C4D7C
conf: Coordinates from Showcaves.com; timeline is a broad Quaternary estimate because the shaft is not dated; Arabic name as given by Showcaves (بئر الطيور is a popular name)

s: Kilometre-long karst depression in the Qara Mountains · one of Arabia’s largest sinkholes
dr: Doline in limestone of the Qara plateau; origin debated, not dated
el: About 1,000 m long, 500 m wide, 250 m vertical range
te: The giant bowl in the mountains
se: A vast bowl about 1 km long sinks into Dhofar’s limestone where two big wadis meet
sa: وعاء هائل يمتد نحو كيلومتر يغوص في حجر ظفار الجيري حيث يلتقي واديان كبيران
desc: A large doline on the karst plateau of the Qara Mountains, Dhofar, about 1,000 m long east–west and about 500 m wide, with a vertical range of 250 m. Its floor lies at about 740 m above sea level, below surrounding hills that exceed 1,000 m. It sits where two large wadis meet, and its floor has numerous swallow holes that drain water underground after rare heavy rains. The official explanation is the collapse of a huge underground chamber; other proposed factors include repeated collapses, widening by wadi water and higher groundwater in a wetter past. It was explored in 1997 by Slovenian cavers and members of Sultan Qaboos University.
sig: A striking example of large-scale karst collapse on the Dhofar plateau.
refs: Duckeck, J. Teeq (Teeq Sinkhole, Teeq Cave), Oman. Showcaves.com. https://www.showcaves.com/english/om/karst/Teeq.html
conf: Coordinates from Showcaves.com; timeline is a broad Quaternary estimate because the depression is not dated; the page notes its origin is uncertain

s: Sea-cave blowholes under a cliff west of Salalah · spouts up to 25–30 m in big swells
dr: Active blowholes over water-filled sea caves
te: Where the sea shoots up through the rock
ta: حيث يندفع البحر من بين الصخور
se: At Mughsail, big waves force sea water up three rock chimneys in tall white fountains
sa: في المغسيل تدفع الأمواج الكبيرة ماء البحر عبر ثلاث مداخن صخرية فتنطلق نوافير بيضاء عالية
desc: At the western end of Mughsail Beach, west of Salalah, an overhanging rock wall known as Marneef Cave shelters three blowholes about 150 m along the trail. Each blowhole is a vertical shaft that opens into a mostly water-filled sea cave below. When large waves strike the cave, compressed air and water are forced up the shafts as fountains reported to reach 25–30 m. The blowholes spout only in heavy swell, so the display is strongest in stormy weather. Mughsail Beach itself is about 6.4 km long.
sig: A clear, visitor-friendly example of wave-driven coastal erosion on Dhofar’s limestone coast.
refs: Duckeck, J. Marneef Cave (كهف المرنيف), Oman. Showcaves.com. https://www.showcaves.com/english/om/caves/Marneef.html
conf: Coordinates from Showcaves.com; timeline is an estimate (Holocene) because the source gives no date for the caves

n: Falaij and Wadi Mahram hyperalkaline springs
na: الينابيع شديدة القلوية في الفليج ووادي محرم
s: Springs of pH above 11 rising from mantle peridotite · natural CO2 capture in action
dr: Active hyperalkaline springs with recent travertine
te: Springs that turn air into stone
se: In Wadi Mahram, water from deep mantle rock is so alkaline that it pulls carbon dioxide from the air and turns it into white stone
sa: في وادي محرم تخرج مياه من صخور الوشاح العميقة شديدة القلوية، فتسحب ثاني أكسيد الكربون من الهواء وتحوّله إلى حجر أبيض
desc: Hyperalkaline springs emerge from the peridotite (mantle) section of the Samail ophiolite at Falaij and in neighbouring Wadi Mahram, in the Wilayat of Samail. Outlet water at Falaij measured pH 11.52–11.63 and 27.9–30.8 °C, and recent travertine was sampled in Wadi Mahram. Such waters react with atmospheric CO2 to precipitate carbonate; across the Oman springs, fresh precipitates date from modern to 350 years and travertine terraces to about 45,000 years. Terraces are typically about 200,000 m² in area and about 1 m thick, growing at about 0.1–0.3 mm per year.
sig: A natural laboratory for mineral carbonation, studied as a model for storing CO2 in peridotite.
ex: Paukert et al. (2012); Falk et al. (2016)
refs: Paukert, A.N., Matter, J.M., Kelemen, P.B., Shock, E.L. & Havig, J.R. (2012). Reaction path modeling of enhanced in situ CO2 mineralization for carbon sequestration in the peridotite of the Samail Ophiolite, Sultanate of Oman. Chemical Geology 330–331, 86–100. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.chemgeo.2012.08.013

Falk, E.S., Guo, W., Paukert, A.N., Matter, J.M., Mervine, E.M. & Kelemen, P.B. (2016). Controls on the stable isotope compositions of travertine from hyperalkaline springs in Oman: Insights from clumped isotope measurements. Geochimica et Cosmochimica Acta 192, 1–28. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.gca.2016.06.026

s: Mantle rock turned completely to carbonate along the ophiolite’s basal thrust
se: Near Fanja, bands of rock that were once mantle peridotite became fully carbonate, locking away huge amounts of CO2
sa: قرب فنجاء تحوّلت أشرطة من صخور كانت يومًا من بيريدوتيت الوشاح إلى كربونات بالكامل، فاختزنت كميات هائلة من ثاني أكسيد الكربون
desc: On a ridge crest just north of Wadi Mansah, about 12 km south-east of Fanjah, peridotite near the base of the Samail ophiolite has been completely carbonated to listvenite (magnesite/dolomite plus quartz). The listvenite bands are about 10 to 200 m thick and run roughly parallel to the banding of the host peridotite along the ophiolite’s basal thrust. Mineral assemblages indicate formation at about 80–130 °C, and clumped isotope thermometry gives about 90 ± 15 °C. An internal Rb–Sr isochron gives 97 ± 29 Ma, linking carbonation to ophiolite emplacement.
sig: Shows that peridotite can be fully carbonated in nature, a key analogue for permanent CO2 storage.
refs: Falk, E.S. & Kelemen, P.B. (2015). Geochemistry and petrology of listvenite in the Samail ophiolite, Sultanate of Oman: Complete carbonation of peridotite during ophiolite emplacement. Geochimica et Cosmochimica Acta 160, 70–90. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.gca.2015.03.014
conf: Coordinates are the centre of the published UTM map extent (zone 40Q, 619,900–625,400 E, 2,582,600–2,587,150 N), converted to latitude/longitude; timeline is the 97 ± 29 Ma uncertainty range; governorate inferred from the location about 12 km SE of Fanjah (Wilayat of Bidbid) and should be checked; Arabic spelling of Mansah is a transliteration

s: Peridotite springs with travertine terraces up to about 45,000 years old
te: Stone steps built by spring water
se: Near Bat, alkaline springs from mantle rock have been building white stone terraces for tens of thousands of years
sa: قرب بات تبني ينابيع قلوية خارجة من صخور الوشاح مدرجات حجرية بيضاء منذ عشرات آلاف السنين
desc: A group of hyperalkaline springs issuing from the peridotite section of the Samail ophiolite west of Al Bana. The outlet waters measured pH 11.65–11.90 and 24.2–32.6 °C, with the highest calcium and the highest Na/Cl (chloride 10.5–12.5 mmol/l) of the Oman springs sampled; along the flow path at Al Bana the water reached 37.7–38.4 °C. Calcium carbonate precipitates where the water meets the air, building a travertine terrace whose radiocarbon ages range from about 15,640 to 44,700 years.
sig: One of the oldest dated travertine records of natural CO2 uptake from Oman’s peridotite springs.
ex: Paukert et al. (2012); Falk et al. (2016)
disc: Travertine up to about 44,700 years old
refs: Paukert, A.N., Matter, J.M., Kelemen, P.B., Shock, E.L. & Havig, J.R. (2012). Reaction path modeling of enhanced in situ CO2 mineralization for carbon sequestration in the peridotite of the Samail Ophiolite, Sultanate of Oman. Chemical Geology 330–331, 86–100. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.chemgeo.2012.08.013

Falk, E.S., Guo, W., Paukert, A.N., Matter, J.M., Mervine, E.M. & Kelemen, P.B. (2016). Geochimica et Cosmochimica Acta 192, 1–28. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.gca.2016.06.026

s: Vast inland sabkha at the edge of the Rub’ al Khali · the Mother of Poisons
dr: Deflation basin formed before 30 ka; arid gypsum/halite crusts since 5.5 ka
el: About 3,000 km² at about 55 m elevation
se: A shining salt flat where the mountains’ water ends its journey, its thin crust hiding treacherous mud
sa: سهل ملحي لامع تنتهي عنده رحلة مياه الجبال، وتخفي قشرته الرقيقة طينًا غادرًا
desc: Umm al Samim is an inland sabkha and groundwater sump of about 3,000 km² at about 55 m elevation, at the south-western foot of the Oman Mountains on the eastern edge of the Rub’ al Khali. It is fed by dune sand, alluvium from the mountains and groundwater from Tertiary Umm Er Radhuma limestone aquifers. The closed depression formed by wind deflation in the gypsiferous Fars Group before 30,000 years ago and has since alternated between saline lake and sabkha phases, with arid capillary gypsum and halite forming since about 5,500 years ago. Its fragile crust over wet sediment earned it the names Mother of Poisons and Mother of Worries; Wilfred Thesiger was the first European to see it, in the late 1940s.
sig: The largest inland sabkha of the Oman foreland, recording desert climate change over the last 30,000 years.
refs: Saltwork Consultants. Umm as Samim, Oman. https://www.saltworkconsultants.com/umm-al-samim-oman/
Wikipedia. Umm al Samim. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Umm_al_Samim
conf: Coordinates are the Wikipedia point for this very large feature (centre of a ~3,000 km² flat); governorate assigned as Ad Dhahirah but the sabkha also extends into Al Wusta; the source gives no governorate

s: Massive sulphide copper ore formed on an ancient seafloor · Samail ophiolite
dr: Massive sulphide deposit in the Samail ophiolite
el: Copper ore of chalcopyrite, pyrite and sphalerite
te: Copper from an ancient sea floor
se: Near Sohar, copper ore that once formed at hot vents on the ocean floor is mined from the mountains today
sa: قرب صحار يُستخرج اليوم من الجبال خام نحاس تكوّن قديمًا عند فتحات حارة في قاع المحيط
desc: Lasail, inland of Sohar in North Al Batinah, is a massive sulphide copper deposit within the Samail ophiolite and an underground mine operated by Oman Mining Company. Its ore and stockwork zones contain chalcopyrite, bornite, cubanite, pyrite, pyrrhotite and sphalerite, with magnetite, hematite, quartz and traces of gold. Studies of the Lasail and nearby Bayda deposits describe hydrothermal mineralisation and alteration of the host basalt in stockwork zones beneath the sulphide bodies. Copper exports from Lasail resumed in 2025 after about 30 years.
sig: A classic example of seafloor hydrothermal copper ore preserved on land in the Samail ophiolite.
refs: Mindat.org. Lasail Mine, Sohar, Al Batinah North Governorate, Oman. https://www.mindat.org/loc-14096.html

Ixer, R.A., Alabaster, T. & Pearce, J.A. (1984). Ore petrography and geochemistry of massive sulphide deposits within the Semail ophiolite, Oman. Transactions of the Institution of Mining and Metallurgy, Section B 93, 114–124.

Global Mining Review (2025). Oman resumes copper exports after a 30-year hiatus. https://www.globalminingreview.com/exploration-development/02012025/oman-resumes-copper-exports-after-a-30-year-hiatus/
conf: Coordinates converted from Mindat’s DMS (24°16′23″N, 56°26′0″E); timeline is the Late Cretaceous range assumed for the ophiolite, not a date from these sources; Arabic spelling لسيل is a transliteration to be checked; export-resumption fact from the news headline

s: Namesake of the largest negative carbon-isotope swing in Earth history · Ediacaran Huqf rocks
dr: Shuram excursion in Oman: onset after 578.2 ± 5.9 Ma, ended by 562.7 ± 3.8 Ma
te: Where the ancient ocean changed its chemistry
se: Rocks in the Huqf desert record a strange global upheaval in ocean chemistry just before the first animals spread
sa: تسجّل صخور صحراء الحقف اضطرابًا عالميًا غريبًا في كيمياء المحيطات قُبيل انتشار الحيوانات الأولى
desc: Wadi Shuram in the Huqf area of central Oman exposes the Ediacaran Shuram Formation, the eponym of the Shuram carbon-isotope excursion, in which carbonate δ13C falls abruptly to about −12‰ worldwide. Measured sections in the wadi were logged with GPS waypoints by Bergmann (2013), including a section of 217 m. Radiometric calibration places the onset in Oman after 578.2 ± 5.9 Ma and its end by 562.7 ± 3.8 Ma, a span of less than 15.5 ± 7.0 million years. The excursion coincides with key steps in the early evolution of animals.
sig: A global reference interval for the Ediacaran carbon cycle and the rise of animal life.
refs: Rooney, A.D., Cantine, M.D., Bergmann, K.D., Gómez-Pérez, I., Al Baloushi, B., Boag, T.H., Busch, J.F., Sperling, E.A. & Strauss, J.V. (2020). Calibrating the coevolution of Ediacaran life and environment. PNAS 117(29), 16824–16830. https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.2002918117

Bergmann, K.D. (2013). Constraints on the Carbon Cycle and Climate During the Early Evolution of Animals. PhD thesis, California Institute of Technology, Appendix C (GPS waypoints). https://thesis.library.caltech.edu/7879/
conf: Coordinates are the base of section WS1 in Bergmann (2013), Table C.1; Arabic spelling of Shuram is a transliteration

na: مقطع القشرة المحيطية في وادي جدعة
s: Reference section through about 6.5 km of fossil fast-spread ocean crust · Samail ophiolite
dr: Fossil oceanic crust of the Samail ophiolite (Wadi Tayin massif)
se: Near Ibra, one valley lets you walk up through a complete slice of the old ocean crust, from deep gabbro to lava
sa: قرب إبراء يتيح وادٍ واحد صعود شريحة كاملة من قشرة محيطية قديمة، من الجابرو العميق حتى الحمم
desc: Wadi Gideah, in the Wadi Tayin massif of the Samail ophiolite near Ibra, exposes a near-continuous section through about 6,500 m of fossil oceanic crust formed at a fast-spreading ridge. A research team sampled the whole profile and analysed the same samples for petrography, petrology, microstructure, thermometry and mineral and whole-rock chemistry. The data show systematic, contrasting compositional trends in the lower and upper gabbros that correlate with stratigraphic depth. The section is used as an on-land analogue and reference for fast-spread lower oceanic crust.
sig: A global reference for how the lower crust of fast-spreading oceans is built.
ex: Garbe-Schönberg et al. (2022); Koepke et al. (2021)
refs: Garbe-Schönberg, D., Koepke, J., Müller, S., Mock, D. & Müller, T. (2022). A reference section through fast-spread lower oceanic crust, Wadi Gideah, Samail ophiolite (Sultanate of Oman): Whole rock geochemistry. Journal of Geophysical Research: Solid Earth. https://doi.org/10.1029/2021JB022734

Koepke, J., Garbe-Schönberg, D., Müller, T., Mock, D., Müller, S. & Nasir, S. (2021). Petrographic features of rock samples of the Wadi Gideah reference profile [dataset]. PANGAEA. https://doi.org/10.1594/PANGAEA.939350

s: Highest summit of the Musandam Peninsula · a sinking carbonate mountain block
dr: Platform carbonates of the Musandam mountains
se: Musandam’s highest peak rises from limestone laid down in ancient seas, in a land that is slowly sinking into the sea
sa: ترتفع أعلى قمة في مسندم من حجر جيري ترسّب في بحار قديمة، في أرض تغوص ببطء في البحر
desc: Jabal Al Harim is the highest mountain of the Musandam Peninsula at 2,087 m, with a prominence of about 1,720 m, about 2.5 km south-east of As Sayh; its southern and eastern slopes feed the headwaters of Wadi Bih. The Musandam mountains are built of a stable-platform succession about 4 km thick, mostly carbonates, deposited from the Permian to the Early Cretaceous, including about 1,500 m of Jurassic Musandam Group carbonates. Today the Arabian plate here is flexed northward beneath Eurasia and subsides by about 6 mm per year, drowning the peninsula’s valleys into fjord-like inlets.
sig: The high point of a carbonate massif whose subsidence created Musandam’s drowned coast.
disc: Region subsiding about 6 mm per year
refs: Wikipedia. Jabal Al Harim. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jabal_Al_Harim

s: Ruins of an 1864 telegraph repeater station in Khor Ash Sham
el: Island about 160 m long and up to 90 m wide
te: The island at the end of the wire
se: On a tiny island in a Musandam fjord, telegraph operators once relayed messages between London and Karachi
sa: على جزيرة صغيرة في أحد أخوار مسندم كان عمّال التلغراف يمرّرون الرسائل بين لندن وكراتشي
desc: A small island in Khor Ash Sham (Elphinstone Inlet), about 160 m long and up to 90 m wide, where a repeater station on the London–Karachi telegraph cable was built in 1864; the Musandam–Bushire section was completed on 25 March 1864. Siemens supplied the equipment and operators’ quarters were built on the island. Extreme heat and isolation made the posting notoriously hard, and the station was abandoned in December 1868 when the cable was diverted to Henjam and Jask. The ruins are now visited by dhow tours and a tourism development project is under way.
sig: A rare surviving landmark of the 19th-century submarine telegraph that linked Europe and India.
refs: Wikipedia. Telegraph Island. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Telegraph_Island

Abbott, L. & Cook, T. (2020). Oman’s Musandam Peninsula: geodynamic and geopolitical nexus. GEO ExPro, 4 December 2020. https://geoexpro.com/omans-musandam-peninsula-geodynamic-and-geopolitical-nexus/
conf: Coordinates from Wikipedia; Wikipedia also mentions abandonment in the mid-1870s, the 1868 date is used here; about 2 km from the existing Khor Ash Sham point but a separate historic site

s: Early 17th-century fort guarding Khasab and the Strait of Hormuz
dr: Built early 17th century; later fortified under Imam Ahmed bin Said Al-Busaidi and Sayyid Said bin Sultan
el: Square plan with four corner towers and a central round tower
te: The fort at the gate of the Gulf
se: A square mud-and-stone fort in Khasab once watched ships passing the Strait of Hormuz
sa: قلعة مربعة من الطين والحجر في خصب كانت ترقب السفن العابرة في مضيق هرمز
desc: A fort in Khasab, Musandam, dated by the Ministry of Heritage and Tourism to the early 17th century (11th century AH), during the reign of Imam Nasir bin Murshid Al-Ya’rubi; another account attributes it to the Portuguese, possibly on an earlier fort. It has a square plan with four corner towers, two floors, one main entrance and a massive circular central tower, its oldest part. It is built of mud, gravel and sarooj, and contains a bait al-qufl and a palm-frond summer house. It served as the governor’s residence, soldiers’ quarters and later a court, and was restored and opened to visitors.
sig: Musandam’s principal historic fort, overlooking the Strait of Hormuz.
ex: Ministry of Heritage and Tourism (Experience Oman); Castles.nl
disc: Central round tower is oldest part
Built of mud, gravel and sarooj

na: مستعمرات الطيور البحرية في جزر مسندم
s: Rugged islands off Musandam with terns, ospreys and tropicbirds · Key Biodiversity Area
dr: Key Biodiversity Area (criterion D1a); last assessed 1994
se: Bare rocky islets off Musandam fill with nesting terns and ospreys above clear blue water
sa: جزر صخرية جرداء قبالة مسندم تمتلئ بطيور الخرشنة والعقبان النسارية التي تعشّش فوق مياه زرقاء صافية
desc: At least 16 rugged, rather barren islands off the Musandam coast and their surrounding seas, covering about 22.5 km² and rising to 70 m, recognised as a Key Biodiversity Area. Jazirat Umm al Fayyarin is the most important seabird breeding island in the region, with terns nesting in significant numbers. The islands hold about 30 pairs of osprey, about 20 pairs of western reef heron on Jazirat Lima, two pairs of sooty falcon and up to 100 red-billed tropicbirds a day, with at least 450 slender-billed gulls in November. Six of the seven most important seabird islands are proposed national nature reserves totalling 630 ha; threats include feral goats, boat disturbance and oil pollution from tanker washings.
sig: The main seabird breeding islands at the entrance to the Arabian Gulf.
disc: Most important seabird island: Umm al Fayyarin
refs: KBA Partnership. Musandam islands (KBA 8215). Key Biodiversity Areas factsheet. https://www.keybiodiversityareas.org/site/factsheet/8215
conf: Coordinates are the published KBA centre point; t0 counts from the 1994 assessment; tern species not named here because the factsheet’s species naming was unclear in the retrieved text

s: Late 13th–early 14th-century fort of the old port city of Sohar · now a museum
se: A white fort by the sea guards Sohar, a port whose ships once carried Oman’s trade across the ocean
sa: قلعة بيضاء على البحر تحرس صحار، الميناء الذي حملت سفنه تجارة عُمان عبر المحيط
desc: Excavations date the fort to the late 13th or early 14th century, when Sohar was under the Kingdom of Hormuz. The Bani Nabhan, known as the Sultans of Sohar, held the city between 1154 and 1634. The Portuguese later modified and used the fort, and Omani forces under Imam Nasir bin Murshid took it from them during the siege of Sohar (1633–1643). Built of mud and whitewash, it was restored from 1985 to 1993 and opened as a historic site and museum in 1993.
sig: The surviving stronghold of Sohar, one of the great historic ports of the Indian Ocean.
disc: Taken from the Portuguese by Imam Nasir bin Murshid
refs: Archnet. Sohar Fort. https://next.archnet.org/sites/22171
conf: Coordinates from the Archnet map marker (approximate); timeline start converted from ‘late 13th century’ (about AD 1290)

s: Early Islamic mosque among ancient copper slag in the Sohar hinterland
dr: Mosque dated 9th–11th century; C-14 dates from slag and kilns of the 6th, 10th and 12th–13th centuries
el: Mosque about 4 × 5.6 m with a semicircular mihrab
se: Among old heaps of copper slag near Sohar, miners once prayed in a tiny mosque with a curved prayer niche
sa: بين أكوام خَبَث النحاس القديمة قرب صحار كان عمّال المناجم يصلّون في مسجد صغير ذي محراب مقوّس
desc: ʿArja lies in the copper-mining hinterland of Sohar in Wadi al Jizzi, where survey and excavation recorded smelting debris and a small mosque of about 4 × 5.6 m with a semicircular mihrab. Pottery and other evidence date the mosque to the 9th–11th centuries, while carbon-14 dates from nearby slag and kilns gave results in the 6th, 10th and 12th–13th centuries. The site was documented in Costa and Wilkinson’s study of the Sohar hinterland.
sig: Links Sohar’s medieval prosperity to industrial-scale copper production in its hinterland.

s: Coastal fort of the Nabhani era, rebuilt under the Al Busaidi state
dr: Dated to 1229 AD (Nabhani era); restored 1984, reopened 1986
se: On the Batinah coast, a big mud fort with four lookout towers still keeps watch over the sea
sa: على ساحل الباطنة ما يزال حصن طيني كبير بأربعة أبراج مراقبة يرقب البحر
desc: Shinas Fort, in North Al Batinah, was built during the Nabhani dynasty, dated by the Ministry to 1229 AD, and rebuilt under the Al Busaidi state as a stronghold and seat of the wilayat’s administration. It is of mud and gravel, about 100 m long, 80 m wide and 8 m high, with four towers up to 9 m used to watch the coast, and five cannons. Inside are a court, school, council hall, stores, guardrooms, a mosque, a central well and a prison. Besieged and partly destroyed in the early 19th century, it was restored by the Ministry in 1984 and reopened in 1986.
sig: A large, well-preserved coastal fort spanning Nabhani to Al Busaidi times.
ex: Ministry of Heritage and Tourism (Experience Oman)

s: Ya’rubi-era fort and seat of the Wali of Liwa · five watchtowers
dr: Built about 400 years ago under the Ya’rubids; restored 2000–2003
se: Surrounded by farms, Liwa’s fort with five towers was home to the governor and his family
sa: تحيط المزارع بحصن لوى ذي الأبراج الخمسة، وقد كان مقرًّا للوالي وأسرته
desc: Liwa Fort in North Al Batinah was built by the Ya’rubids about 400 years ago, under Imam Nasir bin Murshid or Sultan bin Saif. It measures 58 m by 75 m, with high walls, five observation towers and a three-storey central building, Al-Qasbah, that housed the Wali’s family. It served as a defensive structure, the Wali’s residence and the seat of the province’s affairs, and was garrisoned by the army until 2002. Restoration began in 2000 and was completed in 2003, and the fort is open to the public.
sig: A typical Ya’rubi coastal-plain fort that remained an administrative centre into modern times.

s: Historic quarter of the Buraimi Oasis with a rare moated fort
dr: Hamasa over 500 years old; Al Khandaq Fort built by Mutlaq al-Mutayri (r. 1808–13), restored 1994 and 2015–2018
el: Fort ringed by a dry moat
se: In the old Buraimi Oasis, a fort hides behind a deep ditch, a rare defence in Oman
sa: في واحة البريمي القديمة يتحصّن حصن خلف خندق عميق، وهو دفاع نادر في عُمان
desc: Hamasa is a historic quarter of the Buraimi Oasis on the Oman–UAE border, described by the Ministry of Heritage and Tourism as over 500 years old and linked by Falaj Al Jaimi. Al Khandaq Fort stands here, square in plan with four round towers and named after the dry moat that surrounds it, a feature rare in Omani fortification. The Buraimi Oasis Landscape Archaeology Project attributes the fort to Mutlaq al-Mutayri (r. 1808–13) and also recorded Iron Age mounds, aflaj and Late Islamic settlements across the oasis. The fort was restored in 1994 and again between 2015 and 2018.
sig: A rare moated fort at the heart of one of south-east Arabia’s oldest oasis landscapes.
ex: Power et al. (2014); Ministry of Heritage and Tourism
disc: Iron Age mounds in the oasis
